admittedClaims.claimText: PAB's own record for 1924 SPRING GARDEN ST identifies this as "1924 Spring Garden Street."
Baldwin Park's page "Unions in the Neighborhood" states about 1924 SPRING GARDEN ST: "The squat new building at 1924 Spring Garden Street in 1971, built for the Ironworkers Union."
PAB's record shows a historic-register listing entry for 1924 SPRING GARDEN ST, dated 10/11/2000.

Baldwin Park's page "Unions in the Neighborhood" states about 1924 SPRING GARDEN ST: "The International Association of Bridge, Structural, & Ornamental Iron Workers Union Local 401 (founded 1901), which had been at 1924 Spring Garden Street for at least four decades, sold the site to PSSU in 1993."

angleGroups.centralQuestion: What was 1924 Spring Garden Street's role in labor/union history, and how long did that role persist?
angleGroups.perspectiveShift: A plain-looking building constructed in 1971 for the Ironworkers Union was actually the longtime home of a union with roots back to 1901 (Local 401 of the International Association of Bridge, Structural, & Ornamental Iron Workers), which occupied the site for at least four decades before selling it to PSSU in 1993 — turning an unremarkable 'squat new building' into a marker of sustained institutional labor presence in the neighborhood.
